What if chip export controls stop shipments, but not compute?

The overlooked risk in a potential $35 billion AI listing is not chip supply, but customer concentration and regulatory exposure. Nvidia-backed Nscale reportedly generated 73% of last year’s revenue from ByteDance. A

🔧
Reuters (IDC, Oct 12): $NVDA's share of China's data-center AI-chip market fell to 34% in H1 2026 — 678K units, down 44% YoY. Huawei shipped 572K (from ~300K), taking 28%. GPUs fell 26% to 991K of 2.008M total accelerators. Nine of IDC's 11 Chinese chipmakers grew.

My Take 🐉 https://t.co/WFS8wA9lnW

Nvidia's share of China's market for data-center AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground. RTRS

IDC: Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators in China in H1 versus Nvidia's 678,000, which fell 44%. Non-GPU chips now outship GPUs there. Export controls bought time; the useful question is how fast the U.S. uses it.

nvidia shipped 678k AI chips in china in H1 2026, down 44%. huawei shipped 572k, up from ~300k.

per IDC that's 34% vs 28% share.

export controls didn't kill demand, they gave huawei a captive market. how long till devs there stop missing CUDA?

Chinese tech firms bought 1M+ Nvidia gaming and workstation chips, mostly RTX 5090 and RTX Pro, for basic AI workloads, per the FT. Export controls fenced off the flagship cards, so buyers are building clusters from consumer silicon. The controls worked, just not as intended.

Can China bypass chip controls by renting abroad?

Export controls block chips, not access. ByteDance reportedly rented 2,000+ Nvidia AI chips in Norway it can’t import, yielding 73% of Nscale revenue. Rules bar exports, not offshore rentals—should they?
